paper_title: LiveFoley: Dynamic Real-Time Video-to-Audio Generation for Immersive Interactive Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video-to-audio (V2A) generation is essential for immersive interactive applications. However, real-time constraints leave existing streaming V2A methods far behind offline models: (1) visual frontends shrink their receptive fields to cut look-ahead latency, severely degrading audio-visual alignment; (2) causal autoregressive diffusion backends denoise each audio patch in isolation, impairing audio quality. To this end, we present LiveFoley, a streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that addresses both bottlenecks with imperceptible latency. For the visual frontend, we introduce a Trailing Sliding Window that converts non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules without retraining. By simply realigning the window, it preserves precise audio-visual alignment, while a configurable hop size reduces the frontend look-ahead well below the human perceptual threshold. Building on this tunable hop size, we propose the Unified Varhop Framework to accommodate scenarios with diverse latency and computation budgets. For the audio backend, we explore widening the denoising window of the local diffusion transformer (LocDiT) head in two temporal directions. History LocDiT adds past context to improve quality at no latency cost and serves as our default. Alternatively, Future-Warmup LocDiT breaks the autoregressive deadlock with an approximate future condition, further improving generation quality at the cost of an acceptable backend look-ahead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFoley matches offline models in temporal alignment and leads streaming systems in generation quality. Project page: https://dalision.github.io/livefoley-page/

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video-to-audio (V2A) generation is essential for immersive interactive applications. However, real-time constraints leave existing streaming V2A methods far behind offline models: (1) visual frontends shrink their receptive fields to cut look-ahead latency, severely degrading audio-visual alignment; (2) causal autoregressive diffusion backends denoise each audio patch in isolation, impairing audio quality. To this end, we present LiveFoley, streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that addresses both bottlenecks with imperceptible latency. For the visual frontend, we introduce Trailing Sliding Window that converts non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules without retraining. By simply realigning the window, it preserves precise audio-visual alignment, while configurable hop size reduces the frontend lookahead well below the human perceptual threshold. Building on this tunable hop size, we propose the Unified Varhop Framework to accommodate scenarios with diverse latency and computation budgets. For the audio backend, we explore widening the denoising window of the local diffusion transformer (LocDiT) head in two temporal directions. History LocDiT adds past context to improve quality at no latency cost and serves as our default. Alternatively, FutureWarmup LocDiT breaks the autoregressive deadlock with an approximate future condition, further improving generation quality at the cost of an acceptable backend look-ahead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFoley matches offline models in temporal alignment and leads streaming systems in generation quality. Project page: https: //dalision.github.io/livefoley-page/. 1. Introduction In interactive virtual environments, real-time acoustic feedback to user actions is crucial for immersion. While recent world models [24, 44, 59] have advanced synchronized audio-visual generation, their audio synthesis is inherently (a) User study: Figure 1. the minimum audio delay at which participants notice the sound lagging behind the video, for action sounds, speech, and ambient sounds in free roaming (mean 95% CI). (b) Empirical study of streaming visual frontends on the V-AURA [54] backbone: the traditional chunked window (Figure 2a) cuts latency by shrinking the window at sharp cost in audio-visual alignment, while our trailing sliding window (Figure 2b) shortens the hop and preserves alignment. coupled with their internal video generation, rendering them incompatible with external visual pipelines such as game engines, AR/VR, and live camera feeds. In contrast, streaming video-to-audio (V2A) generation presents versatile, source-agnostic alternative by synthesizing audio on-the-fly from arbitrary live pixel streams. Unlike turn-based systems (e.g., GPT-Realtime [37]), streaming V2A requires continuous and precise temporal synchronization, so visual encoding and audio synthesis must jointly execute within an ultralow latency budget to keep the audio-visual delay below the human perceptual threshold. To quantify this perceptual threshold, we conduct user study (Figure 1a; protocol in Appendix A), which reveals two key observations. First, discrete action-sound events (e.g., impacts) are the most sensitive: delays become perceptible at about 0.34 s1, which sets strict latency budget for preserving immersion. Second, the threshold varies sharply with context: delays in speech are perceived at about 0.49 s, whereas ambient sounds during free roaming 1In Appendix A, we compare the difference from ITU-R BT.1359 [21] that our reference-free protocol better reflects real interactive use. 1 are only perceived at about 0.85 s. These findings suggest that an ideal streaming V2A system must (1) achieve high audio-visual alignment and generation quality within an ultra-low latency budget, and (2) dynamically adapt to different scenarios, trading allowable delay for reduced computational load. However, existing streaming V2A approaches cannot achieve imperceptible latency, precise audio-visual alignment, and high audio quality at the same time, owing to two core bottlenecks. The first bottleneck is the look-ahead delay of the visual frontend. Precise audio-visual alignment typically requires segment-level encoders (e.g., Synchformer [20]), but their full segment encoding introduces long look-ahead delay (e.g., 0.64 in V-AURA [54]). Conversely, frame-level encoders (e.g., DINOv2 [38]), as adopted in SoundReactor [45], require only 0.08 frontend look-ahead but severely degrade audio-visual alignment. Our controlled experiment (Figure 1b) further reveals the root cause: as the receptive field of Synchformer shrinks, the audio-visual alignment of downstream generation degrades steadily, showing that alignment hinges on the temporal context each segment covers. The second bottleneck stems from the causal constraints of continuous autoregressive generation. Unlike offline diffusion models that jointly denoise all patches, existing streaming V2A systems [10, 45], built on autoregressive diffusion architectures [22, 29, 61], denoise each patch in isolation with local diffusion or flow-matching head (LocDiT), attending to neither previous nor upcoming patches. As result, these streaming models significantly trail offline systems in audio quality. To address these challenges, we propose LiveFoley, plug-and-play sound engine for general vision-interactive applications that delivers real-time, precisely synchronized, and high-quality acoustic feedback. For the visual frontend, we introduce simple yet effective mechanism, the Trailing Sliding Window, that breaks the latency-alignment tradeoff. Rather than shrinking the receptive field, we anchor the tail of the segment window to the current frame. Paired with first-frame padding, this mechanism converts off-the-shelf non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules, decoupling the frontend look-ahead from the long window length and instead linking it to small, configurable hop size. Building on this tunable hop size, we further propose the Unified Varhop Framework to accommodate the diverse latency and compute budgets of different scenarios (e.g., free roaming vs. shooter games). At its core, Synchronizer module aligns the latent representations across different latency modes, enabling shared generation backbone to adopt dynamic hop sizes. For the audio backend, we explore widening the denoising window of LocDiT beyond single patch. Toward the past, History LocDiT adds previously generated patches as context, improving quality at no latency cost, and serves as our default. Toward the future, the upcoming patch cannot simply join the current denoising window, as its condition depends on the clean current patch, which is not yet available. Future-Warmup LocDiT breaks this autoregressive deadlock by constructing an approximate condition from the current hidden state and the next visual token, enabling cross-patch collaborative denoising. As an optional upgrade, it improves quality further with only 0.08 of extra backend look-ahead, keeping the end-to-end latency at an estimated 236 ms (with hop size = 1, Appendix E), below the human perceptual threshold (Figure 1a). Experiments show that LiveFoley is the first streaming V2A system to match offline models in temporal alignment, with only 0.08 frontend look-ahead, while delivering the best audio quality among streaming systems. On single A800 GPU, it achieves an end-to-end latency below the human perceptual threshold. LiveFoley can thus serve as plug-and-play sound engine for interactive applications such as AR/VR and video games. 2. Related Work Audio-Visual Alignment for Streaming V2A. In offline video-to-audio (V2A) generation, visual representations have evolved from coarse per-frame features, such as CLIP [42, 48], RGB, and optical flow [18], to segment-level features like Synchformer [20]. By substantially improving temporal alignment, this advancement underpins leading offline systems (e.g., MMAudio [4], HunyuanVideo-Foley [47]). In streaming, however, these non-causal encoders introduce latency-alignment tradeoff: V-AURA [54] adopts Synchformer at the cost of 0.64 look-ahead, whereas SoundReactor [45] uses perframe DINOv2 [38] features with minimal look-ahead but weaker alignment. Concurrently, WorldSonus [10] partially mitigates this trade-off by aligning its autoregressive backbone to frozen Synchformer teacher via timeshifted contrastive loss, improving alignment under chunklevel (100 ms) latency but still trailing offline models (Section 4.2). Generative Architectures for Streaming V2A. While global bidirectional diffusion models dominate offline generation [4, 31, 47], streaming applications necessitate autoregressive (AR) architectures to bypass the dependency on full-sequence video inputs. Early AR audio models rely on discrete codec tokens, predicting RVQ token streams autoregressively [6, 27, 35, 54]. However, discrete tokens suffer from quantization loss and require complex scheduling to manage intra-frame dependencies [6, 29]. Recent approaches have therefore shifted toward continuous AR generation, pairing causal LM with local flow-matching or 2 Figure 2. Streaming visual frontend. Each dot denotes the token at one window position. (a) Chunked window: shrinking the window lowers latency but also narrows the receptive field, which degrades audio-visual alignment. (b) Trailing sliding window: anchoring the window tail to the latest frame reduces look-ahead to one hop while preserving the full receptive field and hence the alignment. Black dots are emitted tokens at newly arrived frames. Gray and dashed dots correspond to earlier frames and first-frame padding, respectively; these frames provide context only within the encoder, and their tokens are discarded. (c) Unified Varhop Framework: Synchronizer maps tokens from different hop sizes into shared latent space, allowing single backend to switch among hop sizes. diffusion head [10, 22, 2830, 43, 45, 61]. By eliminating quantization bottlenecks, this continuous paradigm can capture finer acoustic details. Yet streaming V2A models built on this paradigm still fall short of offline models in generation quality [10, 45]. We attribute this partly to their local heads, which denoise each patch in isolation, see history only through the AR hidden state, and cannot denoise jointly with upcoming patches due to causality. Other Online Audio Generation. Beyond streaming V2A, the broader landscape of real-time interactive audio encompasses joint audio-visual generation and acoustic scene modeling. Joint generation models [24, 44, 50, 55, 59] synchronously produce video and audio. However, their audio generation remains strictly coupled to internal video generators, rendering them inapplicable to pre-existing visual streams like game engines or camera feeds. Alternatively, acoustic scene modeling systems [23] focus purely on spatial rendering. These systems adjust the spatial attenuation of static environmental sounds based on user pose, yet cannot generate dynamic action sounds corresponding to transient visual events. In contrast, streaming V2A offers plug-and-play solution that generates synchronized sound directly conditioned on arbitrary dynamic pixel streams, providing maximum flexibility for interactive scenarios. 3. Method 3.1. Preliminaries: Synchformer Synchformer [20] is self-supervised audio-visual synchronization model used as the temporal condition in V2A systems [4, 54]. It splits video into segments of 16 frames (0.64 at 25 fps) and encodes each segment with visual encoder (Motionformer [40]) and an audio encoder i.e., (AST [13]), yielding 8 visual tokens per segment, one every 0.08 s. The encoders are first pretrained with segment-level contrastive objective (Segment AVCLIP), LAVCLIP =

LiveFoley adopts the frozen Segment AVCLIP visual encoder of Synchformer as its frontend. Since attention within segment is bidirectional, token becomes available only after its entire 16-frame segment has arrived; removing this look-ahead without shrinking the receptive field is the goal of Section 3.2. 3.2. Streaming Visual Frontend Chunked Window. Existing streaming V2A methods divide the video into fixed, non-overlapping windows and feed them sequentially to the visual encoder (Figure 2a). For Synchformer, window of tokens spans 2w frames, all of which must be buffered before encoding, so the frontend look-ahead grows linearly with w. Shrinking the window from 4 tokens to 1 cuts it from 0.32 to 0.08 s, but also narrows the temporal receptive field, and downstream audio-visual alignment drops sharply (Figure 1b). The chunked window thus trades alignment for latency. 3 Trailing Sliding Window. The core challenge therefore lies in reducing latency without sacrificing the receptive field w. To this end, LiveFoley introduces trailing sliding window (Figure 2b). Instead of shrinking w, we anchor the tail of the window to the current frame fn, formulating the input sequence as Fn = [fn2w+1, . . . , fn]. By restricting the context to strictly historical frames, this design avoids waiting for full window, decoupling the frontend look-ahead from w. Furthermore, when < 2w, we pad the missing history by repeating the first frame, so that the first output does not have to wait for full window of 2w real frames to accumulate, thereby reducing the end-toend latency. Consequently, this formulation allows off-theshelf non-causal segment-level encoders to operate causally in streaming settings without retraining, while preserving their bidirectional temporal attention. In continuous streaming, the trailing window slides forward as new frames arrive. We introduce hop size that governs the sliding frequency: as illustrated in Figure 2b with Synchformer, the window advances every 2s frames, emitting exactly newly extracted trailing tokens. By adjusting s, we can precisely control the frontend look-ahead τ (e.g., {1, 2, 4} yields τ {0.08, 0.16, 0.32} s). Unlike shrinking the window size w, reducing the hop size keeps the full temporal context, so latency drops while audio-visual alignment is preserved (orange line in Figure 1b). The latency-alignment dilemma thus becomes configurable latency-compute trade-off. 3.3. Unified Varhop Framework As shown in Figure 1a, the tolerable audio delay varies widely across scenarios. Scenarios with strict audio-visual coupling (e.g., shooting or rhythm games) require minimal latency (τ ) and small hop size (s), whereas in ambient scenes (e.g., open-world roaming) delays are only perceived at about 0.85 s, so larger reduces the frontend extraction frequency and saves computation without compromising immersion. Instead of training separate expert model for each hop size, LiveFoley introduces the Unified Varhop Framework (Figure 2c), which supports multiple latency modes with unified model. However, extracting different numbers of trailing tokens from fixed-size window shifts the feature distribution across hop sizes, which can disrupt the downstream audio backend. To map these tokens into unified hidden space, we introduce Synchronizer module to bridge the frontend and backend. Given the 8 tokens R8d of Synchformer window, the Synchronizer produces: Vs = Synchronizer(W )[s :] + emode, (2) where Synchronizer() is two-layer transformer. Rather than directly slicing the trailing tokens from the raw frontend output, this module first incorporates positional embeddings and aggregates intra-window context for global feature alignment. Only then does it slice the final tokens and add learnable latency-mode embedding, emode. The output is constant-rate 12.5 Hz token stream for every hop size, so the audio backend is mode-agnostic and the hop size can be switched per scene at inference. During training, the three hop sizes are rotated in equal proportion across batches, so that single set of weights learns all latency modes. 3.4. Audio Generation Backbone LiveFoley adopts an end-to-end autoregressive diffusion architecture operating on continuous representations from the generacausal audio VAE. As shown in Figure 3, tion module consists of two components: causal language model (LM) and local flow-matching transformer (LocDiT). Operating at 12.5 Hz autoregressive rate, i.e., one step per visual sync token (0.08 s), the acoustic LM captures long-term inter-patch dependencies to produce coarse hidden state hi. Conditioned on hi, LocDiT uses bidirectional attention to refine intra-patch acoustic details. It acts as local denoiser, transforming noise patch x1 = ϵ into clean VAE latent patch x0 , which is fed back to the LM for the next autoregressive step. Superscripts denote flow time, and xi without one refers to patch i. Our framework supports both 16 kHz and 48 kHz causal VAEs, which share the same 12.5 Hz patch rate: the 16 kHz VAE outputs latent frames at 25 Hz and groups = 2 frames into one patch, while the 48 kHz VAE outputs 50 Hz latents with = 4. We describe the 16 kHz variant for simplicity. Causal Acoustic Language Model. Following VoxCPM2 [61, 62], we adopt the MiniCPM [16, 36] architecture as the LM backbone and train it from scratch. To stabilize the continuous autoregressive rollout, we employ LocEnc module [22, 61] that compresses the latent frames of the previously generated patch (x0 i1) into single audio embedding ei1. Since the sync tokens from our visual frontend are already at 12.5 Hz, they are injected without temporal resampling. At step i, the current sync token vi and the previous audio embedding ei1 are linearly projected and concatenated along the channel dimension. The fused representation is then passed through linear layer and fed into the LM to yield the hidden state hi. Local Flow-Matching Head. LocDiT is lightweight diffusion transformer responsible for generating the clean audio VAE patch at the current step. For each denoised VAE token, we construct condition vector ci by concatenating the LM hidden state hi, the current visual sync token vi, and the timestep embedding ϕ(t): ci = Concat(hi, vi, ϕ(t)). In prior streaming V2A work [10, 45], LocDiT denoises each patch in isolation and sees history only through hi; we thus refer to this design as Independent LocDiT (Figure 3, left). Without crosspatch interaction, its bidirectional attention is confined to single patch and lacks sufficient context, which leads to less stable training and poor acoustic quality. 3.5. Widening the Denoising Window Independent LocDiT and global bidirectional DiT (offline) mark the two extremes of cross-patch interaction. Between these extremes, we explore widening the denoising window of LocDiT toward the past and the future (Figure 3, right). Toward the Past: History LocDiT. History LocDiT widens the window unidirectionally toward the past by prepending the previously generated clean patches x0 i2 and x0 i1 to the LocDiT input as context. This gives its bidirectional attention more context and improves generation quality, without introducing extra backend look-ahead. The interaction, however, still flows only from past to present. Toward the Future: Future-Warmup LocDiT. Adding the upcoming patch xi+1 to the window makes the interaction between the current and upcoming patches bidirectional. This inevitably requires vi+1 and thus introduces 0.08 backend look-ahead, which is affordable thanks to the trailing sliding window. However, the fundamental obstacle is an autoregressive deadlock: xi+1 is conditioned on hi+1, which depends on LocEnc(x0 ) and thus cannot be computed while xi is still being denoised in the same window. direct workaround, Low-Rate LocDiT, halves the autoregressive rate so that each step denoises two patches jointly, but it also halves the temporal resolution of the backbone and degrades alignment (Section 4.3). To break the deadlock without lowering the autoregressive rate of the LM, we construct an approximate condition for the future patch by pairing the current LM hidden state hi with the future visual token vi+1: ci = Concat(hi, vi, ϕ(t)), ci+1 = Concat(hi, vi+1, ϕ(t)). (4) This approximation resolves the circular dependency, so the upcoming patch xi+1 can join the current window for joint denoising. Within this window, the two patches interact bidirectionally rather than following strictly pastthe current patch aligns with the acoustic to-future flow: trajectory of the future patch, while the future patch benefits from the context already established by the current one. During training, both xi and xi+1 contribute to the loss. At inference, xi+1 serves only as warmup: it is discarded and regenerated at the next step with the true hi+1. Latency-Quality Trade-off. (4); ()k denotes the output for patch k. The timestep is sampled from logitnormal distribution [8], and all target patches in the same denoising window share single t. To mitigate exposure bias during long-form generation, we apply noise injection [39, 43]: the historical latent patches fed to LocEnc are perturbed with variance-preserving Gaussian noise during training; unlike CALM [43], we also keep small fixed noise level at inference (details in Appendix C). Inference. To support streaming inference beyond the 9.92 training sequences, we adopt an attention sink mechanism [58] with rolling KV cache. The cache retains fixed initial tokens as attention sinks that stabilize attention, while rolling window bounds memory usage. Because KV entries are stored without RoPE [49] and rotary embeddings are applied dynamically based on relative distance, sliding the window reduces to efficient pointer arithmetic and requires no recomputation of historical entries. Training Data. Our training corpus contains about 2,000 hours (745K clips) of in-the-wild and egocentric video. Inthe-wild clips come from SoundAtlas [7], VGGSound [3] and AudioSet [11] corpus filtered for audio-visual consistency; egocentric clips come from EPIC-Sounds [17] and Ego4D-Sounds [2, 14], where we keep clips with high ImageBind [12] audio-visual similarity. The full composition and preprocessing are given in Appendix B. Our main results are evaluated on the standard VGGSound test set for comparability with prior work. However, VGGSound contains many visually unaligned sounds (e.g., offscreen narration and background music) that obscure the differences between visual frontends. We therefore construct VGGSound-Curated, 1,485-clip evaluation subset with strict audio-visual alignment for visual frontend ablation experiments. Candidates are drawn from VGGSoundSparse [19] and VisualSound [54] (ImageBind similarity above 0.3); we exclude clips containing speech or visible faces and keep only valid held-out test clips. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate on 8 clips with the av-benchmark toolkit [4] along four dimensions. Distribution matching is measured by the Frechet distance between generated and ground-truth audio in the feature spaces of PANNs [25] and PaSST [26] (FDPANNs and FDPaSST), and by the KL divergence between PANNs predictions (KLPANNs). Audio quality is measured by the Inception Score (IS) [46] and the production quality score of Audiobox Aesthetics (PQ) [52]. Semantic alignment between video and audio is measured by the ImageBind score (IB) [12], and temporal alignment by the desynchronization score predicted by Synchformer (DeSync) [20]. Implementation Details. The visual frontend is the frozen official Synchformer [20]. We train two causal Oobleck VAEs [9], 16 kHz mono one (25 Hz) and 48 kHz stereo one (50 Hz); with patch sizes of 2 and 4, respectively, the LM runs at 12.5 Hz in both settings. The LM follows the 28-layer MiniCPM [16, 36] architecture and is trained from scratch; LocEnc and LocDiT are 12-layer transformers. Table 1 reports both variants; unless otherwise stated, the ablation studies use the 16 kHz model with = 2. Full architecture, training, and inference details are given in Appendix C. 4.2. Main Results Quantitative Results. Table 1 compares LiveFoley with offline and streaming V2A systems on the full VGGSound test set. Alignment on par with offline models at 0.08 frontend look-ahead: LiveFoley-48k reaches DeSync of 0.48, on par with the offline MMAudio-L (0.47) and far ahead of all streaming baselines (0.67 to 1.03). Best audio quality among streaming systems: LiveFoley-16k obtains the best FDPANNs (9.56) and FDPaSST (92.48) among streaming systems, and LiveFoley-48k the best IS (11.42) among streaming systems and the highest PQ (6.26) of all systems, and the FDPaSST of LiveFoley-16k is second only to offline MMAudio-L (74.16). We attribute this mainly to the continuous-latent backbone and the full-receptive-field visual condition, with History LocDiT further improving FDPANNs (Section 4.3). gap to offline models remains in generation quality: LiveFoley-16k still trails MMAudioL in FDPaSST (92.48 vs. 74.16), FDPANNs (9.56 vs. 8.48), KLPANNs (2.24 vs. 2.18), IS (11.30 vs. 11.62), and IB (0.29 vs. 0.31). Offline models jointly denoise all patches with global bidirectional attention, whereas causal model must commit to each sound from the frames observed so far. Although Future-Warmup LocDiT further narrows this gap by bringing the upcoming patch into the current denoising window  (Table 4)  , closing it under the streaming constraint remains an open direction. Subjective Evaluation. We further conduct listening test on offline and online systems (Figure 4; protocol in Appendix G). The results largely agree with the objective metrics: LiveFoley leads the online systems in both audio quality (MOS-Q 3.23) and audio-visual alignment (MOSA 3.58), and approaches MMAudio-L in alignment (3.79). The exception is MMAudio (online), whose competitive FDPANNs and KLPANNs do not carry over to listening, as the seams of its training-free chunk-wise generation are clearly audible. 4.3. (τ ) Model FDPANNs FDPaSST KLPANNs DeSync 1 (0.08) Expert Unified (ours) w/o Synchronizer 2 (0.16) Expert Unified (ours) w/o Synchronizer 4 (0.32) Expert Unified (ours) w/o Synchronizer 17.07 16.94 17.31 16.36 16.88 16.58 17.04 17.11 16.79 140.22 145.02 147.76 139.88 143.92 146. 143.38 143.33 146.15 1.78 1.90 1.88 1.83 1.86 1.90 1.83 1.82 1.87 0.47 0.47 0.50 0.45 0.46 0. 0.45 0.45 0.47 IB 0.33 0.32 0.32 0.32 0.32 0.32 0.32 0.32 0.31 ical look-ahead. To isolate the visual frontend, we use VAURA [54], widely adopted autoregressive V2A baseline, as the testbed on the VGGSound-Curated subset, keeping all other components identical. Results reveal clear tradeoff in existing methods. Frame-level encoders (e.g., DINOv2 [38], SigLIP2 [53]) require almost no look-ahead but yield poor audio-visual alignment (DeSync > 1.0), despite SigLIP2 providing strong semantics. Conversely, segmentlevel encoders model temporal context for better alignment; for instance, VideoMAE-V2 [56] achieves DeSync of 0.88 but incurs high 0.64 look-ahead. Our proposed trailing sliding window breaks this trade-off, granting Synchformer segment-level alignment at frame-level latency. With only 0.08 look-ahead, it attains superior DeSync of 0.61 while remaining competitive in distribution matching (best FDPaSST and second-best FDPANNs and KLPANNs). Figure 1b further demonstrates the robustness of our method to latency reduction. For the chunked window, we train separate Synchformer for each window size, and train the generation backend conditioned on the features of each model. As the look-ahead drops from 0.32 to 0.08 s, DeSync degrades from 0.67 to 0.88 for the chunked window, whereas it remains nearly unchanged for the trailing sliding window (0.60 to 0.61). Unified Varhop Framework. Table 3 evaluates the Unified Varhop Framework across three predefined hop sizes against independent single-hop experts and Synchronizerfree baseline. The unified model matches the experts in alignment with only minor degradation in distribution metrics, so single shared set of weights can support multiple latency modes and switch hop sizes dynamically during inference. Furthermore, since the visual frontend runs once per window slide, setting = 4 reduces its computational overhead by 4 compared to = 1. Finally, omitting the Synchronizer forces the model to naively slice the final tokens from the raw frontend output, which degrades both DeSync (by about 0.03) and FDPaSST at all hop sizes. This confirms the necessity of the Synchronizer: raw trailing tokens lack the intra-window position and context that its poTable 4. LocDiT ablation on VGGSound-Curated, comparing four denoising window designs under the same backbone. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best scores. LocDiT window FDPANNs FDPaSST KLPANNs IS DeSync IB Independent LocDiT Low-Rate LocDiT History LocDiT Future-Warmup LocDiT 21.08 18.90 17.55 16. 154.62 180.52 158.04 143.92 1.94 2.01 1.92 1.86 12.01 10.38 12.00 12.13 0.47 0.54 0.47 0.46 0.31 0.30 0.32 0.32 sitional embedding and aggregation layers provide. Local Flow-Matching Head. Table 4 compares four denoising windows. Widening toward the past helps: History LocDiT clearly improves FDPANNs (21.0817.55) and IB (0.310.32) over Independent LocDiT, with comparable KLPANNs, IS, and DeSync. Widening toward the future helps further, at an affordable cost: both LowRate and Future-Warmup LocDiT access the upcoming patch and thus introduce an affordable backend look-ahead. With the same window length as History LocDiT, FutureWarmup LocDiT achieves the best distribution and quality scores (e.g., FDPaSST 158.04143.92) and slightly improves DeSync (0.470.46), consistent with the extra visual token it sees. The full rate matters: the halved temporal resolution of the backbone in Low-Rate LocDiT degrades alignment (DeSync 0.54) and FDPaSST (180.52), both worse than Independent LocDiT. 4.4. Deployment and Extensions We further evaluate LiveFoley along two axes. End-to-end latency: at = 1, LiveFoley achieves 156 ms on single A800 GPU, and Future-Warmup LocDiT adds 0.08 (236 ms); both remain below the human perceptual threshold (Figure 1a; Appendix E). Multimodal control: LiveFoley extends to text prompts, with single checkpoint outperforming the state-of-the-art streaming system [10] in both video-only and video-text modes (Appendix F). 5. Conclusion We presented LiveFoley, streaming V2A framework that matches offline models in temporal alignment and narrows the gap in audio quality within human perceptual latency limits. The trailing sliding window turns non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules without retraining, and the Unified Varhop Framework lets single model trade delay for computation. In the backend, History LocDiT adds past patches to the denoising window at no latency cost, while the optional Future-Warmup LocDiT brings in the upcoming patch, further improving quality at 0.08 backend look-ahead that the low-latency frontend makes affordable. With 156 ms end-to-end latency on single A800 GPU, LiveFoley can serve as plug-and-play sound engine for interactive worlds.

VoxCPM2 technical report. arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.06928, 2026. 10 A. User Study on Perceptual Delay Thresholds Table 5. Training data composition. Protocol. This study quantifies the perceptual delay threshold reported in Figure 1a, i.e., the minimum audio delay at which humans notice that the sound lags behind the video. Starting from clips with naturally synchronized sound and visuals, we progressively delay the audio stream by controlled offset and identify the threshold at which participants begin to notice the mismatch. These thresholds serve as conservative latency budget for streaming V2A, under the premise that an imperceptible delay does not disrupt user immersion. We examine three acoustic categories spanning wide range of temporal sensitivity: action sounds synchronized with visible motion, speech, and ambient sound during free roaming. Nine clips (7 8 each) are selected across these categories: three action clips (tennis rally, wood chopping, and trumpet playing), three single-speaker talking-head clips, and three freeroaming scenes, sourced from the VGGSound [3] test set, SpeakerVid-5M [60], and OGameData [1], respectively. Six participants complete the study with headphones, each adopting an active, first-person perspective (imagining performing the on-screen actions) and providing binary response on whether the sound lagged behind the video; actual delay values remain hidden. The perceptual threshold is estimated via an independent adaptive staircase per clip, where the delay increases after an unperceived lag and decreases after perceived one. Testing ranges are 0.10.5 for action, 0.20.8 for speech, and 0.41.0 for ambient scenes, with step sizes of 0.10.2 s. Each staircase terminates after two directional reversals or maximum of eight trials, and trials from different clips are interleaved randomly. complete session involves 3040 trials and lasts 715 minutes. Metric and Results. For each clip and participant, the perceptual threshold is defined as the minimum delay at which the participant reports perceiving lag. We report the mean and standard deviation across clips and participants within each category. Action sounds produce the lowest average threshold at 0.34 0.09 (95% CI over participant means 0.03 s), with the tennis rally at 0.27 (attributed to the sharp transients of ball impacts), wood chopping at 0.39 s, and trumpet playing at 0.42 s. Speech follows at 0.49 0.12 (0.10 s). Free-roaming scenes are tolerated up to 0.85 0.16 (0.10 s), though in 7 of 18 clip-participant staircases the lag remains undetected even at the 1.0 maximum, so this value is lower bound on the true threshold. Paired t-tests confirm all pairwise category differences are significant (p 0.015). Relation to Broadcast Standards. ITU-R BT.1359 [21] reports detectability threshold of about 125 ms and an Source SoundAtlas (VGGSound) SoundAtlas (AudioSet) EPIC-Sounds Ego4D-Sounds Total Domain in-the-wild in-the-wild egocentric egocentric Clips 146K 340K 49K 210K 745K Hours 401 929 134 578 2, acceptability threshold of about 185 ms for audio lagging video. These values are lower than ours, but the two studies measure different quantities and complement rather than contradict each other. BT.1359 asks viewers to compare delayed sequence against an undelayed reference and rate the impairment of lip-synced speech, which yields strict bound for broadcast quality control. In interactive applications, however, no synchronized reference is available, and users judge synchrony from what they see and hear while engaged with the content. Our protocol follows this setting: participants judge each clip without reference and report whether they notice lag, and the content covers action sounds, speech, and ambient scenes. As reference makes small offsets easier to spot, BT.1359 serves as stricter bound, whereas our results reflect when lag becomes noticeable in natural viewing. The default end-to-end latency of 156 ms is acceptable under both views: it is below our measured thresholds and within the acceptability threshold of BT.1359. B. Dataset Details Table 5 lists the composition of our training set. SoundAtlas [7] contributes the VGGSound and AudioSet [11] portions, both filtered for audio-visual consistency. EPICSounds [17] and Ego4D-Sounds [2] provide egocentric footage; from each we keep clips with high audio-visual correspondence measured by ImageBind [12] similarity. All videos are decoded at 25 fps and trimmed to 10 s, and clips are further cropped to at most 9.92 (124 patches at 12.5 Hz) during training. At evaluation, all systems receive the same 25 fps videos, except WorldSonus [10], which is run at 30 fps following its official setup. C. Implementation Details Architecture. The visual frontend is the official Synchformer [20] checkpoint, kept frozen during training. Both audio VAEs adopt the Oobleck architecture of Stable Audio Open [9]: the 16 kHz mono VAE uses temporal downsampling factor of 640 (25 Hz, 64-d latents), and the 48 kHz stereo VAE uses factor of 960 with causal transformer bottleneck (50 Hz, 64-d latents). Each VAE is first pretrained with the standard non-causal recipe and then finetuned after replacing all convolutions with causal ones to Figure 5. Training-free online adaptation of MMAudio (first three ticks shown). At each tick, the pretrained bidirectional flow-matching (FM) model is rerun over its full 8 window, conditioned only on the video that has arrived. Committed audio chunks are pinned during denoising, the next chunk is emitted after the run, and the remaining chunks are discarded and regenerated at the next tick. Dashed arrows indicate that the same initial noise is carried across ticks. avoid look-ahead latency. With patch sizes of 2 and 4 latent frames, respectively, the LM runs at 12.5 Hz in both settings. The LM follows the 28-layer MiniCPM [16, 36] architecture with hidden size of 2048 and is trained from scratch; LocEnc and LocDiT are 12-layer transformers with hidden size of 1024 and 16 attention heads. At inference, the streaming engine runs three-stage asynchronous pipeline (frontend, LM with LocDiT, and VAE decoding) on separate threads. γ η + Training and Inference. We train with AdamW [33] (β = (0.9, 0.99), weight decay 0.05), constant learning rate of 104 after 1K warmup steps, gradient clipping at 1.0, and batch size of 64 clips on 16 A800 GPUs for 200K steps. Classifier-free guidance [15] is trained following DiTAR [22] with condition dropout of 0.1. As data augmentation, the visual condition of LocDiT is dropped with probability 0.1. For the noise injection in Section 3.6, each historical latent patch fed to LocEnc is independently replaced, with probability 0.5, by variance-preserving mix1 γ x0, where γ U(0, 0.5) and η ture = (0, I); the history patches and targets of LocDiT remain clean. At inference, each generated patch is mixed with fixed γ = 0.15 before entering LocEnc, which we find improves generation quality, and we use guidance scale of 6 and 20 Euler denoising steps. For long-form streaming, the LM keeps rolling KV cache of 124 tokens, matching the 9.92 training length at 12.5 Hz, plus 4 attention-sink tokens pinned at the beginning of the stream [58]. Keys are cached without rotary embeddings, and RoPE [49] is applied at attention time from the relative distance between query and key, so evicting the oldest entries requires no recomputation of the remaining cache. D. Online Adaptation of MMAudio MMAudio [4] is an offline flow-matching model that denoises an entire 8 window at once with bidirectional attention, conditioned on the CLIP [42] and Synchformer features of the whole clip. We convert the pretrained 12 MMAudio-L into streaming baseline without retraining, keeping the 8 window and the Euler sampler unchanged; Figure 5 illustrates the procedure. Causal Conditioning. The video is consumed tick by tick, and at each tick only the frames that have arrived are encoded. CLIP features are extracted per frame and Synchformer features per 16-frame (0.64 s) segment; both are extracted incrementally, so each tick encodes only the newly arrived frames and segments. The conditioning sequence retains the length expected by the model: positions corresponding to future frames are filled by repeating the last available token, so no future information leaks in. Because the first Synchformer segment is complete only after 16 frames, the first tick waits 0.64 s, which is the frontend look-ahead reported in Table 1. Committed Prefix with Pinned Denoising. The window does not slide. Generation proceeds in ticks: the first tick starts once 0.64 of video has arrived, and each subsequent tick once further 0.5 has arrived. At every tick, the sampler runs the full Euler trajectory over the entire 8 window, conditioned on the video observed so far and starting from the same fixed initial noise. Latents committed in earlier ticks are pinned in the style of RePaint [34]: at each Euler step they are reset to the forward-noised version of the committed audio at the current timestep, and at the final step to the committed audio itself. After the run, only the latents corresponding to the newly arrived video are committed and decoded, whereas the latents beyond them, which were denoised under repeat-padded conditions, are discarded and regenerated at the next tick. This process repeats until the whole window is committed. Reusing the same initial noise across ticks allows each tick to continue the same underlying sample, which reduces discontinuities at chunk boundaries, although residual seams remain audible in listening tests (Section 4.2). Table 6. End-to-end latency breakdown on single A800 GPU (default setting: History LocDiT, hop = 1). The end-to-end latency is measured with real-time simulator that releases video frames at 25 fps. Composition of the end-to-end latency in the default setting, from the arrival of the first video frame to the output of the first playable audio. The frontend buffers and encodes one hop of video, and the backend runs one LM step, LocDiT denoising, and VAE decoding. The video buffer is the frontend look-ahead τ ; the backend look-ahead (dashed) is zero for History LocDiT and 80 ms for Future-Warmup LocDiT. Block widths are not to scale. Table 7. Frontend look-ahead, backend look-ahead, and end-toend latency for each hop size s, reported as frontend look-ahead (s) / backend look-ahead (s) / end-to-end latency (ms). Only History LocDiT at = 1 (156 ms, bold) is measured; the other latencies are obtained by adding the extra algorithmic look-ahead to this measurement, assuming the same per-patch compute. ments such as 3D game engines and pre-rendered virtual worlds, where audio must be generated at the pace of the rendered frames and no latency budget is available for an external captioner (e.g., VLM) to produce text prompt at inference time. In other content-generation settings, such as generation-based world models, however, text prompt is typically available in advance and can provide useful semantic guidance at no latency cost. In this section, we therefore extend LiveFoley with text as an optional conditioning modality, so that single checkpoint supports both videoonly mode and joint video-and-text mode. Setup. We train text-conditioned variant of LiveFoley. Text supervision is extracted from the per-clip captions provided by SoundAtlas [7]. Text embeddings are produced by frozen Flan-T5 [5] encoder and injected into the generative backbone through cross-attention, similar to WorldSonus [10]. Training mixes text-conditioned and video-only samples, so single checkpoint serves both modes. During inference, each video clip is accompanied by its corresponding text prompt. Results. As shown in Table 8, LiveFoley maintains clear lead over the concurrent WorldSonus in both the video-only and the joint video-and-text modes, on all metrics except KLPANNs with text (1.58 and 1.61 vs. 1.51), confirming that LiveFoley extends naturally to text as an optional conditioning modality. For both models, the semantic guidance from text mainly improves distribution matching (for LiveFoley, FDPANNs 9.617.30 and KLPANNs 2.471.58) at mild cost in audio-visual alignment (DeSync 0.470.50). Participants may freely replay and compare before scoring each output on 5-point Likert scale (1: poor/misaligned; 5: excellent/perfectly aligned) for the two criteria defined below. Metrics. MOS-Q (audio quality). This metric evaluates intrinsic audio quality independent of the video. Raters assess naturalness, clarity, mixing comfort, and the absence of artifacts such as noise or distortion. MOS-A (audiovisual alignment). This metric assesses how well the sound matches the visual content, encompassing semantic and temporal alignment. Semantically, acoustic sources must correspond to on-screen elements (e.g., rain sounding like rain rather than traffic). Temporally, sound events must synchronize precisely with visual actions, such as footstep aligning exactly with foot strike, without noticeable delay or early onset. In summary, MOS-Q measures standalone audio fidelity, whereas MOS-A evaluates coherence between the audio and visual modalities. Results. Figure 4 in the main paper summarizes the subjective evaluation results. Among online systems, LiveFoley consistently outperforms the baselines across both criteria, achieving MOS-Q of 3.23 (compared to 2.79 for MMAudio (online), 2.75 for V-AURA, and 3.04 for WorldSonus) and MOS-A of 3.58 (surpassing 3.15, 3.02, and 2.96, respectively). Notably, WorldSonus operates at comparable frontend look-ahead (0.10 s) yet trails LiveFoley most clearly in alignment. Compared with offline models, LiveFoley approaches MMAudio-L in audio-visual alignment (3.58 versus 3.79), though gap in audio quality remains (3.23 versus 3.62). While AudioX achieves an audio quality comparable to LiveFoley, it receives the lowest alignment score (1.90), corroborating its high DeSync (1.22) in Table 1.
